zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check, after independent scan reading: the supplied *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan-based transcription and English notes are this reviewer's work; the index is not a diplomatic authority.

runs.text: dadas a cada tempo, como folguedos, &c.

lines.note: Dadas completes acõmo-dadas at the end of f394: pleasing things suited to each occasion, such as festivities. The repeated catchword on the preceding page is not duplicated as an extra body row here.
Qiodacu means consenting or agreeing. The scan has an upright terminal S., a written-usage label separate from the italic gloss.
Tçuyoqi and vôqinari explain strength and greatness. The caron over the headword's o and the circumflex in vôqinari are visibly different and are preserved separately.
Grande completes the strong-and-large definition. The separate upright S. closes this sense before the next similarly spelled headword.

Cagamino dai identifies the base or stand of a mirror. The initial letters are Qio, not the OCR's Quo; no clear accent is printed over this headword's o, so none is supplied despite the neighboring accented forms. The supplied NINJAL index identifies this entry as Qiǒdai, but that lexical spelling does not establish an accent in this impression.
This Qiǒdai is glossed as brother. The scan prints the caron over o and the Portuguese nasal ending, distinguishing the row from the preceding mirror-stand entry.

runs.text: Modo de falar differente que ha em

lines.note: Qiǒdan introduces differences in regional speech. The Japanese starts Qiǒ-, not Quǒ-, and the Portuguese visibly has differente, including the i omitted by OCR.

runs.text: varios reinos, ou prouincias onde ſe falla a

lines.note: The definition specifies different kingdoms or provinces in which the same language is spoken. The double l in falla is retained as printed rather than standardized.

runs.text: meſma lingua, mas he algũa palaura differẽte,

lines.note: The language is the same, but an individual word can differ. The nasal abbreviations in algũa and differẽte are retained without spelling them out.
Pronunciation can differ as well; Cuni qiǒ-dande gozaru introduces an example of regional speech. The division after qiǒ- is physical and does not indicate a separate word.
Dande gozaru completes the Japanese example. The Portuguese says it is the manner of speaking of that particular region, with the noun supplied below.
Reino completes the explanation as the speech of that kingdom or province. This single word closes the dialect entry before Qiǒdana.
Qiǒdana is a shelf or table for books. The source's Parteleiro and tightly set deliuros are preserved rather than silently modernized or respaced.
Qiǒden is defined as a book. Its short one-word gloss is complete here, with a caron on the Japanese o.
Qiodô is illustrated by Qioxu dôſocu, raising the hands and moving the feet. The scan has circumflexes in Qiodô and dôſocu; the Portuguese explanation continues on the next row.
This completes the gesture example, lifting the hands and moving the feet. The source's unaccented double-e pees is retained.

Qiǒfai and the alternative qeifai concern reverence and worship, also expressed by Vyamai and vogamu. The printed lowercase l introduces an alternative, not an erroneous i; the first headword's Q is damaged but identifiable.
Neração completes Veneração, followed by adoração. Both terms belong to the reverence-and-worship entry rather than forming an independent row of vocabulary.
Qiǒfendo denotes places or villages near the capital. The partly broken initial is roman Q, not the OCR's italic O; the place name completes the sentence below.

Miyaco completes the Portuguese phrase referring to settlements near the capital. Although a Japanese place designation, it is printed in italic within the Portuguese explanation and is flagged for optional whole-word typeface review.
Mutçuqi identifies cloth used for wrapping an infant or catching its excrement. The scan distinguishes the caron in Qiǒ- from the circumflex in -fô and divides the Portuguese wrapping verb at embu-.

runs.text: rulhão a criança, ou com que lhe tomão os ex-

lines.note: Rulhão completes the source's emburulhão, wrapping the child; the alternative concerns catching the child's excrement. Ex- continues on the next row, with the historical wrapping-verb spelling preserved.
Crementos completes excrementos and the cloth definition. The final upright S. is the written-usage label, not part of the italic word.
Curǔ votto explains a mad or deranged man, with the historical Portuguese gloss Doudo. The headword has dotted i, not OCR r, and ends in an upright S. usage label after the gloss.
Qiǒgai concerns a domain or object of perception, illustrated first by colour. The repeated Japanese glosses Sacai and ſacai are retained rather than collapsed as an apparent duplication.

runs.text: & luz dos olhos, ſom dos ouidos, &c.

lines.note: Light is associated with the eyes and sound with the ears, completing the examples of perceptual objects. The printed ouidos is preserved without modern accentuation.

A further sense is the human body, followed by a quotation beginning Sangai fi-roxito. The Japanese must be read with f, whose cross-stroke is visible on enlargement: firoxi means broad, agreeing with largo below, not the OCR's ſiroxi.

The quotation says that although the world is broad, there is no place to set a small human frame. Roxito completes firoxito; voqi- continues with docoro on the next row, and the source's goxacu measure is not normalized.
Docoro naxi completes the lack of a place to stay. Feiq. is the upright source citation; the Portuguese translation begins 'although this world', dividing abbreviated mũ-do across the row boundary.

runs.text: do he largo, todauia não tenho lugar pera por,

lines.note: The world is wide, yet the speaker has nowhere to put or accommodate the body. Do completes mũdo, and the source's unaccented por is retained.

runs.text: ou agaſalhar hum corpo do tamanho de ſete pal-

lines.note: The gloss describes sheltering a body of seven spans or less, expressing the quotation's small human frame in Portuguese units. Pal- is the printed division of palmos.
Mos completes palmos and the qualification 'or less'. This closes the quotation and body sense before the next headword.
Qiǒguan denotes books or writings. The initial sequence is Qiǒ-, not OCR Quǒ-, and the Portuguese word starts eſ-, not oſ-.
Qiôguat means last month. The headword's circumflex is visible, and the source's Mes is retained without adding a modern accent.
Qiǒguen is explained by playful or mad speech and glossed as comic interludes. The Japanese form and Portuguese theatrical term are preserved rather than replaced with modern genre labels.
The scan includes a pilcrow omitted by OCR. Qiǒguenuo yǔ, alternatively ſuru, means performing the comic pieces; lowercase l introduces the alternative verb and en- begins entremeſes.
Tremeſes completes entremeſes and the performance example. This continuation is not a separate headword.
Qiǒguendayǔ denotes the chief performer or master of these comic interludes. The final long-u mark is retained and the objects of faz continue below.
The chief performer presents interludes or farces. Both Portuguese terms complete the preceding definition rather than identifying additional Japanese entries.
Qiǒguenxa is assigned the same meaning as the preceding performer term. Idem points backward to Qiǒguendayǔ, not forward to the following falsehood entry.
Qiogui is equated with Soragoto and glossed as a lie. The faded opening is Qio, not the OCR's M, supported by the visible letter sequence and the falsehood entries that follow.
Qiogo is explained by speaking falsely and by Soragoto. The initial Y in Ytçuuari is retained rather than replaced with the I used elsewhere in the dictionary.
The Portuguese confirms a lie; the Japanese example says that a lie does not ultimately remain intact or succeed. The paragraph mark and the doubled t in mattacarazu are retained.

runs.text: A mentira por derradeiro não medra por q̃ lo

lines.note: The gloss explains that a lie does not prosper in the end, because it is soon discovered. The source divides logo as lo/go without a hyphen at this right edge.
Go completes logo and the explanation that the lie is discovered. This is an indented continuation, not a fresh unindented entry; the final S. is upright.
Qiogon shares the preceding sense of falsehood. The broken initial Q remains identifiable, and Idem is the entire Portuguese gloss.

Qiogin means establishing an encampment, explained by Ginuo ſuyuru and the Portuguese military-camp gloss. The partly broken opening reads Qio-, not OCR ho-; the crop has been raised to include the complete surviving Q.

The final row supplies the example Qiogin ſuru, establishing camp. It is an indented body continuation with italic Vt. and otherwise roman Japanese, not the OCR's fragmented Vi. Qogn iuru or page furniture.

Miyacono vchi means inside the capital, also expressed by the Portuguese phrase containing Miaco. The source's different spellings Miyaco and Miaco are both retained; the latter is an embedded place name for optional typeface review.
Qiogiǔ denotes residence or a stay, without an o accent in this headword. Naga- starts the example place name Nagasaki, divided between physical rows.
The example means residing in Nagasaki. The Portuguese phrase is Estar de aßento, being settled somewhere; the visible double-s type gives aßento, not the OCR's aſtento.

The translation ends 'live in Nagasaki'. The nasal abbreviation in the printed Nãgaſaqui is preserved; this place name occurs within the Portuguese sentence and is flagged for optional whole-word typeface review.
Caruxi and vomoxi contrast light and heavy. This homograph concerns relative weight or gravity rather than the preceding residence sense, and its o carries a caron.
Peſada completes the weight contrast. The example applies it to the gravity of an offence, with xitagatte expressing conformity to that degree.
Tçumini voconǒ completes the example of imposing punishment according to the offence. The Portuguese abbreviations alguẽ and cõforme are left unexpanded.

runs.text: à graueza, ou leueza do peccado.

lines.note: Punishment is proportioned to the seriousness or lightness of the offence or sin. The double c in peccado and the printed accent on à are retained.
Qiojacu denotes weakness or something lacking vigour. The Portuguese adds strength on the next physical row before introducing examples.
The first example is Qiojacuna miacu, a weak pulse. Fra- is the visible division of fraco; it does not begin a separate example or entry.

runs.text: co de peßoa que eſtà muito debilitada, & fra-

lines.note: The pulse belongs to someone very debilitated and weak. The source repeats the fra- division, now completing fraca on the following row, and the grave accent in eſtà is retained.
Ca finishes the description of the debilitated person. A second example, Qiojacuna fito, then describes a weak person, with a further qualification below.
The person is also without vigour. This closes the second example of Qiojacu and is not part of the next headword's initial gloss.
Qiojacuna is the adjectival form, weak or debilitated. Vi- begins the Portuguese cross-reference instruction Vide on the next row.
De completes Vide, directing the reader back to Qiojacu. The Japanese cross-reference target is upright after the italic instruction and is flagged for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Hum inſtrumento de metal como tenta

lines.note: Qiǒji denotes a metal implement compared to a probe. Its purpose is given in the following row; no modernized tool name is substituted for the printed tenta.

runs.text: com que calcão a cinza do perfumador. Vt,

lines.note: The implement is used to tamp down the ashes in an incense burner. The row closes with italic Vt, introducing a paired expression on the next row.

The pair Qiǒji, coji is explained as this implement together with Faxis used for the fire. Faxis occurs within the Portuguese sentence, unlike the standalone Japanese pair, and is flagged for optional whole-word typeface review.
The Faxis serve to stir or stoke the fire. This is a continuation of the implement-pair explanation, not a new entry.
Qiǒjin is equated with Monogurui and glossed as a mad or deranged person. The Japanese synonym after i is not an embedded term in the Portuguese gloss.
Itçuuari and macoto contrast falsehood and truth. The initial I is retained as printed, differing from Ytçuuari in column 1, and the second Portuguese member continues below.
Verdade completes the lie-and-truth pair. This short row closes Qiojit before the document entry.

runs.text: Papel eſcrito que hum apreſenta ao ſe-

lines.note: Qiojǒ is a written paper presented to a lord in a dispute. The first Q is part of the headword despite wide type spacing; ſe- begins ſenhor on the following row.

runs.text: nhor com prouas, & teſtimunhas ſobre algũa

lines.note: The paper is presented with proofs and witnesses concerning a claim. Nhor completes ſenhor; the nasal abbreviation in algũa remains over u.
Demanda completes the description of the claim or dispute supported by the paper, proofs, and witnesses. This closes Qiojǒ.
Qiǒman denotes pride or arrogance; Qiǒman ſuru gives the corresponding action. The example's long ſ and the paragraph mark are visible.
The one-word Portuguese verb means becoming proud or behaving arrogantly. It translates the Japanese example immediately above, not a separate headword.
Qiomei is equated with Muxit and defined as false testimony or defamation. The headword's o is unaccented, and in- begins infamia across the row boundary.
Famia completes infamia. The example concerns bringing a false accusation against someone; the printed iycaquru is retained rather than respelled from modern Japanese, and Im- begins Impor.

runs.text: por, ou aleuantar a alguem falſo teſtemunho.

lines.note: Por completes Impor, followed by the alternative of raising false testimony against someone. The wording confirms the defamatory sense of the preceding example.
Cǒbaxij agiuai explains a fragrant or pleasant taste. The printed agiuai and the separate long-o carons are retained, with the final Portuguese quality supplied below.
Cheiroſo completes the pleasant-and-fragrant taste description. The following S. is upright and labels written usage.

runs.text: Liuros da ley, & doutrina que eſ-

lines.note: Qiǒmon denotes books of religious law and doctrine. The dictionary attributes them to Xaca on the next row; eſ- is the printed division of eſcreueo.

Creueo completes eſcreueo, followed by Xaca, the Japanese name for Shaka, the Buddha. The name is embedded in the Portuguese sentence and appears in its italic type; the OCR's mixed-font split inside Xaca is removed and the whole name is flagged for review.
Sannuru toxi and Cozo both identify last year. The Portuguese begins the same explanation with O anno, retaining the printed double n.
Paßado completes O anno paßado, last year. This short continuation belongs to Qionen and is not an independent entry.
Qionet is described historically as a slow or lingering fever. This is the dictionary's period definition, whose explanation of its origin continues below, not a modern medical assessment.

runs.text: de hum eſtar fraco, ou debilitado.

lines.note: The historical gloss associates the fever with being weak or debilitated. The scan includes a faint b in debilitado, omitted by OCR; no medical inference is added beyond the source's statement.

runs.text: Certa mezinha que ſe faz do miollo

lines.note: Qiǒnin names a historical medicinal preparation made from a fruit-stone kernel. The scan reads miollo, including the o before the doubled l, not OCR millo; the fruit is identified below.
The kernel is that of an apricot stone. The old Portuguese albicorque is retained, and this description records the dictionary's historical use rather than recommending the preparation.
Qiǒqi is explained by Curǔ qi and the historical Portuguese word Doudice, madness or derangement. This sense is distinct from the waking-with-a-start homograph below.
Vodoroqi, voquru supplies the Japanese forms for starting or waking in alarm. The source's initial v forms are preserved; the Portuguese explanation continues with the suddenness of the action.

The gloss describes getting up suddenly in fright. The worn word is eſpantado, supported by its surviving letters and the alarm sense, not the OCR's separated eſpante do; derepente remains one printed word.
Qiǒqijin denotes a mad or deranged person. The damaged initial is Q rather than OCR D, and the row is a complete independent entry.
Caramomono fana identifies the flower of a particular peach-like fruit tree. The native crop has been raised to include the full initial Q; the botanical comparison is completed below.

The dictionary compares the tree with a peach and an apricot. This is an indented continuation of Qiǒqua, not a separate unindented entry; the period botanical wording is retained without imposing a modern species identification.

Qiôqiô concerns fear and reverence, explained by Voſore, uru. Both o marks are circumflexes; the crop has been raised to preserve the full Q. The Portuguese reuerẽ- continues beyond the page and is anticipated by the separate catchword cia.
The final small sort is read as the signature numeral 2; its ink-heavy lower stroke resembles a lowercase a. The catchword is separate at the right edge.
